summary: This informational memo describes the Host Identity namespace, a cryptographic namespace for applications, and the Host Identity Protocol layer between internetworking and transport layers. It supports end-host mobility, multihoming and NAT traversal. It obsoletes RFC 4423 and addresses concerns raised by the IESG, including crypto agility.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally a computer is known by where it sits. This document describes a way to name computers by a secret-based identity instead, so that a laptop can move around and still be recognised, and so that two machines can prove who they are without relying on addresses that change.

questions: what is a host identity tag
subtitle: An architecture that names computers by a public key instead of by where they are plugged in.

tldr.problem: IP addresses are used both as the name of a host and as its location, so a host that moves, sits behind a NAT or changes networks is hard to reach and hard to authenticate.
tldr.mechanism: The Host Identity namespace uses a public key as the name of a host. A Host Identity Protocol layer between the internetworking and transport layers binds transport associations to those identities and uses IP addresses only as locators.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9063 is an informational architecture memo that obsoletes RFC 4423. Its own deployment analysis says HIP has not been a wild success in the Internet.

today: RFC 9063 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 4423, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it. Its own deployment analysis says HIP has not been a wild success in the Internet, with low demand and substitute technologies preferred, although it has been deployed in an industrial control network and in a security product.

sections.title: Introduction: Names for Machines, Not Places
sections.content:
The Internet has two important global namespaces, IP addresses and DNS names. These have powered the Internet to what it is today, and they also have weaknesses, because semantic overloading and functionality extensions have greatly complicated them. The proposed Host Identity namespace is also a global namespace, and it fills an important gap between the IP and DNS namespaces.

A Host Identity conceptually refers to a computing platform, and there may be multiple such identities per platform, because the platform may wish to present a different identity to different communicating peers. There is exactly one Host Identifier for each Host Identity, although there may be transient periods such as key replacement when more than one identifier is active. The Host Identifier is the public key of an asymmetric key pair, and each Host Identity uniquely identifies a single host. If two or more computing platforms have the same Host Identifier, they are instantiating a distributed host. The Host Identifier can be public, for example published in the DNS, or unpublished, and client systems will tend to have both.

There is a subtle but important difference between Host Identities and Host Identifiers: an identity refers to the abstract entity that is identified, while an identifier refers to the concrete bit pattern used in the identification process. Although Host Identifiers could be used in many authentication systems, the architecture introduces a new protocol, the Host Identity Protocol, and a cryptographic exchange, the HIP base exchange. HIP provides for limited forms of trust between systems, enhances mobility, multihoming and dynamic IP renumbering, aids in protocol translation and transition, and reduces certain types of denial-of-service attacks.

When HIP is used, the payload traffic between two HIP hosts is typically, but not necessarily, protected with Encapsulating Security Payload, and the Host Identities are used to create the needed security associations and to authenticate the hosts. When ESP is used, the actual payload IP packets do not differ in any way from standard ESP-protected IP packets. The document expands Host Identities beyond their original use to enable IP connectivity and security, and to enable general interhost secure signaling at any protocol layer, where the signal may establish a security association between the hosts or simply pass information within the channel.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is simple: give every computer a name that is really a cryptographic key. The key stays the same when the machine moves, and holding the matching secret key is what proves the machine is who it claims to be.

sections.title: Background: What the Current Namespaces Cannot Do
sections.content:
The Internet is built from three principal components: computing platforms, packet transport infrastructure, and services. All of these need to be named in order to interact in a scalable manner, and the document concentrates on naming computing platforms and packet transport elements. There are two principal namespaces for this: IP addresses and domain names. Domain names provide hierarchically assigned names for some computing platforms and some services, each hierarchy is delegated from the level above, and there is no anonymity in domain names.

The IP addressing namespace has been overloaded to name both interfaces and endpoints. In their role as interface names, IP addresses are sometimes called locators and serve as an endpoint within a routing topology. IP addresses are numbers that name networking interfaces, typically only when the interface is connected to the network. Originally, IP addresses had long-term significance, but today the vast number of interfaces use ephemeral or non-unique addresses, because every time an interface is connected to the network it is assigned an IP address.

The document identifies three critical deficiencies with the current namespaces. First, establishing initial contact and sustaining data flows between two hosts can be challenging because of private address realms and the ephemeral nature of addresses. Second, confidentiality is not provided in a consistent, trustable manner. Finally, authentication for systems and datagrams is not provided. All of these deficiencies arise because computing platforms are not well named with the current namespaces.

An independent namespace for computing platforms could support end-to-end operations independent of the evolution of the internetworking layer, and could support rapid readdressing of that layer because of mobility, rehoming or renumbering. If it is based on public-key cryptography it can also provide authentication services, and if it is created locally without registration it can provide anonymity. The namespace should be applied to the IP kernel or stack, should fully decouple the internetworking layer from the higher layers, should not mandate any administrative infrastructure, should have a fixed-length representation, should be affordable in packet size and computation, should avoid name collisions, should provide a localized abstraction for use in existing protocols and APIs, should allow names to be created locally, should provide authentication services, and should produce names that are long-lived but replaceable at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: Today one number does two jobs: it says which machine you are and where you are. Because addresses are handed out when a device connects and taken back when it leaves, a machine that moves is a machine with a new name, and there is no way to prove from the address alone who is on the other end.

sections.title: The Host Identity Namespace
sections.content:
A name in the Host Identity namespace, a Host Identifier, represents a statistically globally unique name for naming any system with an IP stack. A system can have multiple identities, some well known, some unpublished or anonymous, and may self-assert its own identity or use a third-party authenticator such as DNSSEC, PGP or X.509 to notarize the assertion. In the HIP architecture, the public key of a private-public key pair has been chosen as the Host Identifier because it can be self-managed and it is computationally difficult to forge. Since authenticated datagrams are mandatory to provide much of HIP's denial-of-service protection, the Diffie-Hellman exchange in the base exchange has to be authenticated, so only public-key Host Identifiers and authenticated HIP messages are supported in practice. Non-cryptographic forms are referenced but should only be used where there is no risk of host spoofing and no use of ESP, and for interconnected networks spanning several operational domains the set of environments where that risk is acceptable is the null set.

The actual Host Identifiers are never directly used at the transport or network layers. Instead, a Host Identity Tag is used in other protocols to represent the Host Identity, and a Local Scope Identifier is another representation that can be used in protocols and APIs.

A Host Identity Tag is a 128-bit representation created from a Host Identity Hash, an IPv6 prefix and a hash identifier. Its fixed length makes for easier protocol coding and better manages packet size cost, and it presents the identity in a consistent format independent of the cryptographic algorithms used. In essence, the HIT is a hash over the public key, and the two algorithms that affect its generation are the public-key algorithm and the hash algorithm, both encoded in the bit presentation of the HIT. Through HIPv2, the second preimage resistance is 96 bits, less than the 128-bit width of an IPv6 address field because of the ORCHID prefix. Ninety-six bits was considered acceptable during the design of HIP but may eventually be insufficient, and deployments that do not use ORCHIDs might use the full 128-bit width.

A Local Scope Identifier is a 32-bit localized representation, suitable for use in the existing sockets API in place of IPv4 addresses without modifying applications. LSIs are never transmitted on the wire: when an application sends data using a pair of LSIs, the HIP layer translates them to the corresponding HITs, and back again on receipt. LSIs help legacy IPv4 applications keep working over IPv6-only networks. Their main disadvantage is their local scope, because applications that pass LSIs to each other in application-layer protocols may be describing an entirely different host, though the document notes the LSI concept is effectively a host-based NAT and does not introduce more issues than the ubiquitous middlebox NATs.
sections.plainLanguage: The real name is a long public key, but that is too big to put in a packet header, so it is shortened to a fixed 128-bit tag that stands for it. Locally, a short 32-bit number stands in for the same identity so that old programs can keep working without knowing anything about HIP.

sections.title: The New Stack: Separating Names from Locations
sections.content:
The IP addresses currently embody the dual role of locators and endpoint identifiers: each IP address names a topological location, acting as a routing direction vector or locator, and at the same time names the network interface currently located at the point of attachment, acting as an endpoint name. In the HIP architecture the endpoint names and locators are separated. IP addresses continue to act as locators and the Host Identifiers take the role of endpoint identifiers. A Host Identity can be simultaneously reachable through several interfaces, so endpoint names based on Host Identities are slightly different from interface names.

Architecturally, HIP provides for a different binding of transport-layer protocols: TCP connections and UDP associations are no longer bound to IP addresses but rather to Host Identities. In practice the Host Identities are exposed as LSIs and HITs for legacy applications and for the transport layer, to keep existing networking APIs and stacks working. The HIP layer is logically located at Layer 3.5, between the transport and network layers. It acts as a shim layer for transport data using LSIs or HITs, and translates between the two forms of HIP identifier and routable IPv4 or IPv6 addresses in both directions.

A host may have multiple identities on both the client and the server side. For security reasons it may be a bad idea to duplicate the same Host Identity on multiple hosts, because the compromise of a single host taints the identities of the others, so a unique identity per host is advisable. At the server side, using DNS is a better alternative to a shared Host Identity for load balancing, since a single fully qualified domain name entry can refer to multiple Host Identities. Instead of duplicating identities, HIP opportunistic mode can be used, where the Initiator leaves out the identifier of the Responder and learns it when the exchange completes; the trade-off is lower security guarantees, but it avoids publishing Host Identifiers in any directory, which makes it suitable for peer-to-peer connectivity. A host may also hold multiple identities for privacy reasons, or to use different identities for different administrative domains.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP sits between the transport and network layers. The transport layer now talks about identities, and HIP does the translation to an IP address for each packet, and back again when the reply comes. That is what lets a machine change address without breaking the conversation.

sections.title: The Control Plane: Base Exchange, Mobility and Relays
sections.content:
HIP decouples the control and data planes. Two end hosts initialize the control plane using a key exchange procedure called the base exchange, which can be assisted by HIP-specific infrastructural intermediaries called rendezvous or relay servers. In the event of IP address changes, the end hosts sustain control plane connectivity with mobility and multihoming extensions, and eventually they terminate the control plane and remove the associated state.

The base exchange is a key exchange procedure that authenticates the Initiator and the Responder to each other using their public keys. It consists of four messages during which the hosts also create symmetric keys to protect the control plane with hash-based message authentication codes. Those keys can also be used to protect the data plane, and IPsec ESP is typically used as the data plane protocol. Both the control and data planes are terminated with a closing procedure consisting of two messages. The base exchange also includes a computational puzzle that the Initiator must solve; the Responder chooses the difficulty of the puzzle, which permits it to delay new incoming Initiators according to local policies, for instance when it is under heavy load. The puzzle design allows the Responder to remain stateless until the very end of the base exchange, which offers some resiliency against denial-of-service attacks.

After the initial key exchange, the HIP layer maintains transport-layer connectivity using its mobility and multihoming extensions, so HIP can provide a degree of internetworking mobility and multihoming at low infrastructure cost. A system is considered mobile if its IP address can change dynamically for any reason such as PPP, DHCP, IPv6 prefix reassignment or a NAT device remapping its translation, and multihomed if it has more than one globally routable IP address at the same time. HIP links addresses together when several correspond to the same Host Identity, so that if one address becomes unusable existing transport associations can be moved to another. When a mobile node moves during an ongoing communication, it sends a HIP UPDATE packet to inform the peer of the new addresses, and the peer then verifies that the node is reachable through them.

Establishing contact with a mobile node is more involved, since the Initiator has to know how to reach it. HIP provides the rendezvous mechanism, in which the mobile node keeps the rendezvous infrastructure continuously updated with its current addresses, as an alternative to depending on dynamic DNS. The rendezvous mechanism is especially useful when both nodes change address at the same time, because the UPDATE packets would cross in the network and never reach the peer. The relay mechanism is an alternative, more suitable for IPv4 networks with NATs, because a HIP relay can forward all control and data plane communications to guarantee successful NAT traversal.
sections.plainLanguage: Two machines first run a four-message handshake that proves who they are and agrees keys. After that, a machine that changes address tells the other with an UPDATE message. When a machine is behind a NAT, a relay server can pass the messages through for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the Deployment Reality
sections.content:
The security considerations section covers man-in-the-middle attacks, protection against flooding attacks, the use of Host Identity Tags in access control lists, alternative Host Identifier considerations and trust on first use. The document also notes that the zones and identifiers involved are subject to the same caveats as any cryptographic naming scheme, and that the puzzle mechanism, the authentication of the base exchange and the separation of identifiers from locators are the parts that carry the protection. This document obsoletes RFC 4423 and addresses the concerns raised by the IESG, particularly crypto agility, and it incorporates lessons learned from the implementations of RFC 7401.

The appendix on deployment and adoption sets out the costs. An additional layer and a namespace always involve some initial effort in implementation, deployment and maintenance. HIP introduces a need to manage Host Identifiers and to manage HIP-aware endpoints at scale: what were formerly IP address-based access control lists become trusted HITs, and the mappings between HITs and IP addresses, as well as access policies, must be managed. Because HIP decouples the identifier and locator roles of IP addresses, a mapping mechanism is needed to associate them, and a failure to map a HIT to its locator may result in failed connectivity, because a HIT is flat by its nature and cannot be looked up from the hierarchically organised DNS. From the performance point of view, HIP control and data plane processing introduces some overhead in throughput and latency, and the key exchange introduces two extra round trips in the initial connection establishment between two hosts, although subsequent TCP sessions using the same HIP association do not bear that cost within the key lifetime.

The deployment analysis reports that HIP has been adapted and deployed in an industrial control network in a production factory and has been included in a security product to support Layer 2 VPNs, but that HIP has not been a wild success in the Internet. From a marketing perspective the demand for HIP has been low and substitute technologies have been favoured. Some technical misconceptions related to the early stages of the HIP specifications still persist, in particular that HIP does not support NAT traversal and that HIP must be implemented in the operating system kernel; both claims are untrue. In a minimal setup a client and a server machine have to run HIP software, and DNS records for HIP are usually set up to avoid manual configuration, while rendezvous servers and firewalls are optional, and no changes are required to network address points, NATs, edge routers or core networks, although HIP may require holes in legacy firewalls.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is honest about the outcome. HIP solves real problems, and it has been used in a factory network and in a security product, but it has not caught on widely, mostly because the demand was low and other technologies were preferred instead.
